\chapter{Colours}
\label{ch:colours}
\hlchaptermodality{16}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can name four basic colours in French, put a colour after the noun it describes, and say which of them are not Latin.}

Four colours with two different homelands. noir walked down from Latin niger and rouge from a root older than Latin — the same one behind English red, rust and German rot. But blanc and bleu are Frankish, Germanic words that displaced Latin ones inside a Romance language, which is the opposite of the usual traffic. albus did not die when blanc took its job; it stopped being a colour and became l'aube, the dawn. And the colour goes after its noun — le vin rouge — with bonjour as the exception the reader already says every day.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[noir]{noir — black}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-noir}



\begin{quote}
Four colours in this chapter, and they do not have four similar stories. Start with the one that behaves exactly as you would expect, so the surprises stand out later.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-oi} — the \textbf{oi} is \emph{wa}, one gliding vowel. It is the same \textbf{oi} you have in \textbf{trois} and \textbf{soir}.
  \item \texttt{r-uvular} — the final \textbf{r} is sounded here, made in the throat.
  \item Together: \textbf{noir} = \emph{NWAR}, one syllable.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{noir} is Latin \textbf{niger}, \textquotedblleft{}black.\textquotedblright{} Nothing was borrowed and nothing is hiding: the word walked straight down from Rome into French, and did the same into its sisters — Spanish \emph{negro}, Italian \emph{nero}.

English took \emph{niger} too, but only as a metaphor. To \textbf{denigrate} someone is, literally, to \textbf{blacken} them — to darken a name rather than a thing. The colour stayed in the Romance languages; the insult is what crossed into English.

So \emph{noir} is the plain case. Hold on to that, because the next colour is not plain at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}noir\textquotedblright{} — \emph{NWAR}, the \emph{oi} a single gliding vowel
  \item the family — \textquotedblleft{}niger, noir, negro, nero\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English one — \textquotedblleft{}denigrate: to blacken a name\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say black? (\textbf{noir}, \emph{NWAR}.) What Latin word is it from? (\emph{\textbf{niger}}.) What does \textbf{denigrate} literally mean? (To \textbf{blacken} — to darken someone's name.) Next: white, which did not come from Latin at all.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[blanc]{blanc — white}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-blanc}



\begin{quote}
Every word in this book so far has come down from Latin. This one did not, and the direction it came from is the opposite of what usually happens.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{nasal-an} — the \textbf{an} is the nasal vowel you have in \textbf{janvier}.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — the \textbf{c} at the end is \textbf{not} pronounced.
  \item Together: \textbf{blanc} = \emph{BLA(N)}, one syllable, nothing after the nose.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin had a perfectly good word for white: \textbf{albus}. French does not use it.

\textbf{blanc} is \textbf{Frankish} — a \textbf{Germanic} word, from \emph{*blank}, meaning not \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{} exactly but \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{shining, gleaming, flashing}.\textquotedblright{} The Franks are the people who gave France its name, and they gave it its word for white as well.

That direction is the surprising part. Latin words pour into Germanic languages constantly; English is more than half built of them. Traffic the other way, a Germanic word displacing a Latin one \textbf{inside} a Romance language, is much rarer.

Why did \emph{albus} lose? Most likely because \emph{blank} was more \textbf{vivid}. \emph{Albus} is a flat, plain white; \emph{blank} is a white that \textbf{shines}. Colour words are replaced by the more dramatic option surprisingly often — the exciting word wins and then calms down into the ordinary one.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}blanc\textquotedblright{} — \emph{BLA(N)}, the \emph{c} silent
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}noir, blanc\textquotedblright{}
  \item the origin — \textquotedblleft{}Frankish blank: shining\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two stories — \textquotedblleft{}noir walked down from Rome, blanc walked in from the north\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say white? (\textbf{blanc}, \emph{BLA(N)}.) Is the final \textbf{c} sounded? (\textbf{No.}) Which language did it come from? (\textbf{Frankish} — Germanic, not Latin.) What did \emph{*blank} actually mean? (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{Shining}, gleaming.\textquotedblright{}) What was the Latin word it displaced? (\emph{\textbf{albus}}.) Next: where \emph{albus} went instead.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[l'aube]{l'aube — the white that stopped being a colour}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-aube}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Blanc} took the job. That does not mean \emph{albus} was thrown away — words that lose an argument usually go and do something else.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{albus} is still all around you. It simply stopped being the word for the colour, and survives inside words for \textbf{things that are white}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{l'aube} — the \textbf{dawn}: the sky going white. French, and pronounced \emph{lohb}
  \item \textbf{l'aubépine} — the \textbf{hawthorn}, literally the \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{white thorn}\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{album} — English, from a \emph{blank white tablet} you wrote on
  \item \textbf{albino} — English, someone white-skinned
\end{itemize}

That is a pattern worth naming, because it will keep happening. When a newer word takes over a plain everyday meaning, the older one does not vanish. It gets pushed into the \textbf{specific} — a time of day, a particular tree, a technical term — and stays there for centuries, unnoticed.

So French has two whites after all. One you say when you mean the colour, and one you say without knowing you are saying it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}l'aube\textquotedblright{} — \emph{lohb}, the dawn
  \item the white inside it — \textquotedblleft{}albus: the sky going white\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English survivors — \textquotedblleft{}album, albino\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two whites — \textquotedblleft{}blanc for the colour, aube for the hour\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{l'aube} mean, and what is white about it? (The \textbf{dawn} — the sky going white.) Which Latin word is inside it? (\emph{\textbf{albus}}.) Name two English words that kept the same \emph{albus}. (\textbf{album}, \textbf{albino}.) What happens to a word when a newer one takes its everyday job? (It survives in the \textbf{specific} — a time, a tree, a technical term.) Next: red, which is older than Latin.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[rouge]{rouge — red}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-rouge}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Noir} came from Latin and \emph{blanc} from the Franks. This one goes back further than either — further than Latin itself.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-ou} — the \textbf{ou} is the pure \textbf{oo} you have in \textbf{douze}.
  \item \texttt{soft-j} — the \textbf{g} here is the soft \emph{zh} of \emph{measure}, the same sound as the \textbf{j} in \textbf{janvier}.
  \item Together: \textbf{rouge} = \emph{ROOZH}, one syllable. English borrowed the word whole for makeup and kept the French sound with it.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{rouge} is Latin \textbf{rubeus}, \textquotedblleft{}reddish.\textquotedblright{} But \emph{rubeus} is itself inherited, from a Proto-Indo-European root \textbf{*h\textsubscript{1}rewd\textsuperscript{h}-} so old that its children are scattered across the whole family:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item Latin \emph{ruber}, \emph{rubeus} $\to$ French \textbf{rouge}, and English \textbf{ruby}, \textbf{rubric}
  \item English \textbf{red}, \textbf{rust}, \textbf{ruddy}
  \item German \textbf{rot}
\end{itemize}

So \emph{rouge} and \textbf{red} are not lookalikes that happen to mean the same thing. They are \textbf{actual cousins}, separated for something like five thousand years and still saying the same colour.

That is not an accident of this one word. \textbf{Red} is one of the oldest colours any language names — after black and white, it is almost always the third colour a language gets a word for, and often the only other one for a long time. A word that old survives everywhere because it was never not needed.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rouge\textquotedblright{} — \emph{ROOZH}, the soft \emph{g}
  \item the cousins in a row — \textquotedblleft{}rouge, red, rot\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Latin ones — \textquotedblleft{}ruber, ruby, rubric\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three you have — \textquotedblleft{}noir, blanc, rouge\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say red? (\textbf{rouge}, \emph{ROOZH}.) How is the \textbf{g} pronounced? (Soft — the \emph{zh} of \emph{measure}.) Are \emph{rouge} and English \emph{red} borrowed from each other? (\textbf{No} — they are \textbf{cousins} from the same Proto-Indo-European root.) Name two more of that root's children. (\textbf{rust}, \textbf{ruddy}, \textbf{ruby}, \textbf{rubric}, German \textbf{rot} — any two.) Next: blue, which went abroad and came home.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bleu]{bleu — blue}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-bleu}



\begin{quote}
The fourth colour, and the second one that is not Latin. Once is a curiosity; twice is a pattern about who was actually living in France.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-eu} — the \textbf{eu} is the rounded front vowel you made in \textbf{sœur}: lips rounded, tongue forward.
  \item \texttt{silent-final} — there is no consonant after it to say.
  \item Together: \textbf{bleu} = \emph{BLUH}, one syllable, and shorter than English speakers expect.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bleu} is \textbf{Frankish *blāo} — Germanic again, borrowed exactly the way \emph{blanc} was.

Then something neat happened. \textbf{English took \emph{bleu} from French.} So English \textbf{blue} is a Germanic word that walked into France, spent centuries there changing its shape, and was then borrowed back into a Germanic language. It went abroad and came home wearing different clothes.

Meanwhile German never sent its copy anywhere: it still says \textbf{blau}, which is what \emph{*blāo} sounded like all along. Say \textbf{blau}, \textbf{bleu}, \textbf{blue} in a row and you are hearing one word at three stages of one journey.

\emph{(French has a second, more poetic blue as well — \textbf{azur}, ultimately from Arabic }lāzaward\emph{, \textquotedblleft{}lapis lazuli.\textquotedblright{} You have almost certainly seen it already, on the map: the \textbf{Côte d'Azur}.)}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bleu\textquotedblright{} — \emph{BLUH}, lips rounded, and keep it short
  \item the round trip — \textquotedblleft{}blau, bleu, blue\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two Frankish ones — \textquotedblleft{}blanc, bleu\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four — \textquotedblleft{}noir, blanc, rouge, bleu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say blue? (\textbf{bleu}, \emph{BLUH}.) Which language did it come from? (\textbf{Frankish} — Germanic, like \emph{blanc}.) What is odd about English \textbf{blue}? (It is a \textbf{Germanic} word that English borrowed \textbf{from French} — it went abroad and came back.) What did German keep? (\textbf{blau}.) Next: where the colour goes in the sentence.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[le vin rouge]{le vin rouge — where the colour goes}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-vin-rouge}



\begin{quote}
You have four colours and a table full of nouns. Putting them together takes one rule, and English gets it the other way round.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the colour comes second}]
English puts the colour \textbf{in front} of the noun: \emph{red wine}, \emph{white bread}. French puts it \textbf{behind}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{le vin rouge} — the wine red
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{le pain blanc} — the bread white
\end{quote}

The order feels backwards for about a week and then stops feeling like anything. What makes it stick faster is noticing that you \textbf{already say the exception}.

\textbf{bonjour} is \emph{bon} + \emph{jour} — a good day, with the adjective in \textbf{front}. So French does both, and the split is not random: a small handful of very common, very short adjectives go before the noun — \emph{bon}, \emph{bonne}, and a few others you will meet — while nearly everything else, \textbf{colours included}, goes after.

That is the useful form of the rule. Not \textquotedblleft{}French adjectives follow the noun,\textquotedblright{} which the word \emph{bonjour} would immediately contradict, but: \textbf{the short common ones lead, and everything else follows.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two wines — \textquotedblleft{}le vin rouge, le vin blanc\textquotedblright{}
  \item with bread — \textquotedblleft{}le pain blanc\textquotedblright{}
  \item the exception you already own — \textquotedblleft{}bonjour: bon comes first\textquotedblright{}
  \item the rule as one line — \textquotedblleft{}short and common in front, everything else behind\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}le vin rouge, le vin blanc\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}red wine\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{le vin rouge} — the colour \textbf{second}.) White bread? (\textbf{le pain blanc}.) Which everyday word puts its adjective \textbf{first}? (\textbf{bonjour} — \emph{bon} + \emph{jour}.) State the rule in one line. (\textbf{Short, common adjectives go in front; everything else, colours included, goes after.}) Next: the three colours on the flag.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[bleu, blanc, rouge]{bleu, blanc, rouge — the flag}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-tricolore}



\begin{quote}
Three of your four colours are the flag, and saying them in its order is the easiest way to keep them. There is also a joke buried in them.
\end{quote}

\begin{culture}
The French flag is named by its colours, left to right:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{bleu, blanc, rouge}
\end{quote}

Say it in that order and it comes as one unit rather than three words. French speakers say it that way constantly — \emph{le drapeau bleu-blanc-rouge} — and it is by far the most common context in which all three appear together.

Now count where they came from:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{bleu} — Frankish, Germanic
  \item \textbf{blanc} — Frankish, Germanic
  \item \textbf{rouge} — Latin, from a root older than Latin
\end{itemize}

So the \textbf{tricolour is two-thirds Germanic}. The flag of the most self-consciously Latin nation in Europe names itself with two borrowed Germanic words and one inherited one, and no one notices, because a word stops being foreign the moment everybody uses it.

That is the honest summary of this chapter: of four basic colours, \textbf{half} came from the north. Half of French's most everyday vocabulary is not doing what the label \textquotedblleft{}Romance language\textquotedblright{} would lead you to expect.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the flag — \textquotedblleft{}bleu, blanc, rouge\textquotedblright{}
  \item all four colours — \textquotedblleft{}noir, blanc, rouge, bleu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the sources — \textquotedblleft{}Latin, Frankish, Latin, Frankish\textquotedblright{}
  \item the finding — \textquotedblleft{}the tricolour is two-thirds Germanic\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}bleu, blanc, rouge\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name the flag's colours in order. (\textbf{bleu, blanc, rouge}.) Which two of them are Germanic borrowings? (\emph{\textbf{bleu}} and \emph{\textbf{blanc}}.) So what fraction of the tricolour is Germanic? (\textbf{Two-thirds.}) And of the chapter's four colours? (\textbf{Half.}) Next: all four, put to work.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — four colours and where they came from}

\label{lesson:FR-C13-practice}



\begin{quote}
Four words, and then the thing that makes them worth more than four words: each one has a passport.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the four}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}noir, blanc, rouge, bleu\textquotedblright{}
  \item the flag order — \textquotedblleft{}bleu, blanc, rouge\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two nasal ones — \textquotedblleft{}blanc\textquotedblright{}; and the two that end in a vowel sound — \textquotedblleft{}bleu\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}noir, blanc, rouge, bleu\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: put them on nouns}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le vin rouge, le vin blanc\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}le pain blanc\textquotedblright{}
  \item the order out loud — \textquotedblleft{}the noun, then the colour\textquotedblright{}
  \item the exception — \textquotedblleft{}bonjour\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: where each one came from}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}noir — Latin niger; denigrate\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}blanc — Frankish blank, shining\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}rouge — Latin rubeus; red, rot, ruby\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bleu — Frankish blao; blau, bleu, blue\textquotedblright{}
  \item the one that changed jobs — \textquotedblleft{}albus became l'aube, the dawn\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{four colours}, and the flag as a set.
  \item \textbf{word order} — the colour goes \textbf{after} the noun, and \emph{bonjour} is the exception you already said before you knew it was one.
  \item \textbf{half of them are not Latin.} \emph{blanc} and \emph{bleu} are Frankish, which runs against the usual direction of traffic: Latin words flood into Germanic languages, not the reverse.
  \item \textbf{a word that lost and survived anyway} — \emph{albus} gave up the colour and kept the dawn. That is what usually happens to a displaced word, and it is worth looking for.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the four colours. (\textbf{noir, blanc, rouge, bleu}.) Which two are Germanic? (\emph{\textbf{blanc}} and \emph{\textbf{bleu}}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}red wine.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{le vin rouge} — the colour second.) Which Latin word for white did French drop, and where did it end up? (\emph{\textbf{albus}} — in \textbf{l'aube}, the dawn, and in English \emph{album} and \emph{albino}.) Are \emph{rouge} and \emph{red} borrowed from each other? (\textbf{No} — \textbf{cousins}, from one Proto-Indo-European root.)
\end{tcolorbox}
